## Reproducibility — what is it?

::: {.fragment}
### "U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) subcommittee on replicability in science: 'reproducibility refers to the **ability of a researcher to duplicate the results of a prior study using the same materials as were used by the original investigator.'**"

![](https://blog.ml.cmu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/2.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

<small><em>Goodman et al., Science Translational Medicine 01 Jun 2016: Vol. 8, Issue 341, pp. 341ps12. DOI: 10.1126/scitranslmed.aaf5027</em></small>
:::

## We are in a reproducibility crisis in science

![](libs/Images/RepoCrisis.png){fig-align="center"}

<small><em>Monya Baker (2016). 1500 scientists lift the lid on reproducibility. Nature 533 (7604).</em></small>

## Types of reproducibility

<small><em>From Victoria Stodden (as summarized in the ROpenSci Reproducibility Guide)</em></small>

::: {.fragment}
"**Computational reproducibility**: when detailed information is provided about code, software, hardware and implementation details."
:::

::: {.fragment}
"**Empirical reproducibility**: when detailed information is provided about non-computational empirical scientific experiments and observations. In practice this is enabled by making data freely available, as well as details of how the data was collected."
:::

::: {.fragment}
"**Statistical reproducibility**: when detailed information is provided about the choice of statistical tests, model parameters, threshold values, etc. This mostly relates to pre-registration of study design to prevent p-value hacking and other manipulations."
:::

## A few areas for improvement

::: {.incremental}

- Tedious & time consuming for a collaborator to recreate the analyses
- Backed up w/version control? Probably not…
- How do we transfer this into a final report or presentation? Is that reproducible?

## FAIR and CARE principles

![](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5d3799de845604000199cd24/1567592451970-2R8XFL670QNMAGDRV7ED/Be+FAIR+and+CARE.png?format=2500w){fig-align="center"}

## CARE principles for Indigenous Data Governance

![](libs/Images/CARE.png){fig-align="center" width="45%"}

Jennings et al. 2023

## CARE principles, close to home

CARE stands for **Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility,** and **Ethics** — a complement to FAIR that centers the rights and interests of the people data is *about*, not just those reusing it.

::: {.incremental}
- **Collective Benefit**: data ecosystems should be designed to benefit Indigenous communities, not just researchers or institutions
- **Authority to Control**: Native Hawaiian communities and organizations (e.g., DAR, DHHL, community-based monitoring groups) have the right to govern data about their ʻāina, moʻolelo, and resources
- **Responsibility**: researchers must build relationships that support the self-determination of Kānaka Maoli and local communities before, during, and after data collection
- **Ethics**: data practices should reduce harm and actively consider Native Hawaiian and Pacific values, not just legal compliance
:::

## CARE in practice, here in Hawaiʻi

::: {.callout-note}
## Data governance is already happening locally
**DHHL** and **OHA** maintain their own protocols for who can access and use data about Native Hawaiian beneficiaries, lands, and resources — a real-world example of Authority to Control. If your research touches Hawaiian Home Lands, ceded lands, or Kānaka Maoli communities, identify and respect these structures **before** you collect a single data point.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## Why this matters for your Community Data Sprint
Working with DAR, DOH, or a Mālama restoration group in Week 8 means handling data tied to a specific place and community. CARE asks who benefits, who decides, and who's accountable — not just whether the data is technically open.
:::
:::

## Git and GitHub

Why use it?

Do you have a folder for your research project that looks like this?

::: {.center}
![](https://njsilbiger.github.io/images/Week1/BadDirectory.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}
:::

## Git and GitHub solve this problem

### Git
- Git is a distributed version control system.
- Imagine if Dropbox (saving info on the cloud) and "Track changes" from MS word had a baby. Git would be that baby.
- But, it's even better because Git is optimized for the things that data scientists spend a lot of time working on (e.g., code)
- There is a learning curve, but I promise you it is worth it.

::: {.fragment}
### GitHub
- Git and GitHub are two different things.
- GitHub is an online hosting platform that provides an array of services that are built on the Git system. (There are also other platforms like Bitbucket and GitLab)
- Just like we don't *need* RStudio to run R code, we don't *need* GitHub to use Git... but it will make our lives a lot easier

<small><em>https://raw.githack.com/uo-ec607/lectures/master/02-git/02-Git.html</em></small>
:::

## From software development...

Git and GitHub play a big role in global software development.

- There is a high probability that your fave app., program or package is built using Git-based tools (RStudio is).

::: {.fragment}
### ... to scientific research
- Git and GitHub help operationalise the ideals of open science and reproducibility
- Journals have increasingly strict requirements regarding reproducibility and data access. GH makes this easy (DOI integration, off-the-shelf licenses, etc.)
- I host all my code, data for my research papers, and research protocols on GH.
- GH helps us to collaborate with others and, most importantly, **your future self.**
:::

### Push (pizza)

## Most important commands

**Pull** - `git pull` — this "downloads" any changes to your repository on GitHub, by your collaborators, or your past self on a different machine. (always do this first! You may have forgotten that you made a change.)

::: {.fragment}
**Add** - `git add` — this stages files. It tells git, "I want to add these to the repository"
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Commit** - `git commit` — this "saves" your changes with git (as opposed to ctrl+S which saves them to your local machine – although you should still do that too)
:::

::: {.fragment}
- git commit always requires a message so that you know what changes you made.
- ex: `git commit -a -m "I created a test repo"`
- "-a" means commit all (every change) "-m" means (I am adding a message). What you have in quotes is your message.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Push** - `git push` — this "uploads" your changes to GitHub.
:::

## Work with git in the terminal

::: {.incremental}
- First, let's create and save a simple script (save it as "testscript.R")
- Now, let's save it to git
- Click on the terminal tab (next to console). This allows you to interact directly with your terminal
- Type "git pull" (it should say already up to date because you have not done anything yet)
- Type `git add testscript.R` (this stages the new script)
- Type `git commit -a -m "I am adding testscript"`
- Type `git push`
  - you may get prompted for your username and password
:::
